interactions.summary: Jiang clarifies that Purgatory-shortening prayer is not casual; the intensity, duration, and communal scale of living prayer all matter.
A student reads Canto 4 on absorbed attention and unnoticed time, and Jiang uses it to restate that emotional capture, not clock perception, governs lived time in Purgatory.

claims.claim: Jiang says committed prayer can reduce a soul's purgatorial delay, and that both the amount of devotion and the number of people praying matter.
Canto 4 states that when delight or pain grips the soul, time continues physically but is not perceived because another faculty has seized the whole mind.
Jiang interprets this as a distinction between physical time and emotional time: what binds the soul emotionally matters more than noticing the sun's progress.
The class links loss of time-perception to ordinary experiences of absorption, happiness, and change, extending the poetic claim into lived psychology.

signature_moments.moment: Clock-time has no force if the emotions have already taken the whole mind hostage.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It restates Jiang's purgatorial time theory in a more psychological idiom.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture folds Manfred's prayer economy back into the broader emotional-time model: both intercession and duration are measured through lived force rather than mere chronology.
